cards.front: How much oxygen does each decilitre of blood release from hemoglobin between the lungs and the tissue?
cards.back: Carrying capacity (about 20 mL per dL when fully loaded) times the fall in saturation: capacity × (saturation in the lungs − saturation in the tissue).
cards.quote: oxygen released from hemoglobin = capacity × (saturation in the lungs − saturation in the tissue)

cards.front: Why does hemoglobin's S-shaped dissociation curve suit one carrier that must both load in the lungs and unload in the tissues?
cards.back: It keeps saturation in the lungs near full yet lets saturation in the tissues fall far, so the same carrier loads fully and still unloads a lot.
cards.why: Over the resting range a one-site carrier cannot both load fully and unload a lot.
cards.quote: Hemoglobin's S-shaped curve keeps the first saturation near full and lets the second fall far, so one carrier loads fully and still unloads a lot.

cards.front: In adult human blood, arterial PO2 is near 100 mmHg and blood returning from resting tissues is near {{c1::40}} mmHg.
cards.back: In hard exercise, mixed or regional venous PO2 can approach 20 mmHg.
cards.quote: with arterial blood near 100 mmHg and blood returning from resting tissues near 40 mmHg

cards.front: Why does almost all the oxygen in adult human blood ride on hemoglobin rather than dissolved in plasma?
cards.back: Dissolved oxygen is only about 0.003 mL per dL per mmHg, about 0.3 mL per dL at 100 mmHg, against about 20 mL per dL bound to fully loaded hemoglobin.
cards.quote: Dissolved oxygen is about 0.003 mL per dL for each mmHg, only 0.3 mL per dL at 100 mmHg
cards.section: Where the points sit on the curve

cards.front: Adult hemoglobin (HbA) has four chains, {{c1::two alpha and two beta}}, and four oxygen-binding sites.
cards.quote: the predominant adult human form, HbA, has four chains (two alpha and two beta) and four oxygen-binding sites
cards.section: Where the points sit on the curve

cards.front: What is P50 on an oxygen dissociation curve, and does a higher P50 mean higher or lower affinity?
cards.back: The PO2 at which hemoglobin is half saturated. A higher P50 means lower affinity.
cards.why: A carrier that grips tightly is already half full at a low pressure.
cards.quote: a tight grip is half full at a low pressure, so a higher P50 means lower affinity
cards.section: Where the points sit on the curve

cards.front: In a standard model of human blood at 37 degrees C, pH 7.4 and a carbon dioxide pressure of 40 mmHg, P50 is about {{c1::26.8}} mmHg.
cards.quote: In a standard model of human blood at 37 degrees C, pH 7.4 and a carbon dioxide pressure of 40 mmHg, P50 is 26.8 mmHg.
cards.section: Where the points sit on the curve

cards.front: On the adult human oxygen dissociation curve, where do the loading plateau, the resting unloading point and the reserve sit?
cards.back: Nearly flat above about 60 mmHg (loading plateau). Resting blood at 40 mmHg sits on the shoulder. The steep part, about 10 to 35 mmHg, is the reserve for hard work.
cards.quote: so the resting point at 40 sits on the shoulder and the steep middle is the reserve for hard work
cards.section: Where the points sit on the curve

cards.front: In the standard model of adult human blood, saturation changes by about 0.07 percentage points per mmHg at 100 mmHg and about 1.3 per mmHg at 40 mmHg. Estimate the fall in saturation for a 5 mmHg drop in PO2 at each point.
cards.back: At 100 mmHg: 0.07 × 5 ≈ 0.35 points. At 40 mmHg: 1.3 × 5 ≈ 6.5 points, nearly twenty times more.
cards.why: The plateau protects loading in the lungs; the shoulder and steep middle let tissue PO2 changes release oxygen.
cards.quote: saturation changes by about 0.07 percentage points per mmHg at 100 mmHg, about 1.3 at 40 mmHg and about 2.6 near 25 mmHg.
cards.section: Shoulder and reserve, by slope

cards.front: State the Fick principle for whole-body oxygen use.
cards.back: At steady state, oxygen use = cardiac output × (arterial oxygen content − mixed venous oxygen content).
cards.quote: At steady state, the Fick principle says oxygen use is cardiac output times the arterial-minus-mixed-venous difference in content.
cards.section: How much oxygen does the body use?

cards.front: Blood oxygen content (mL per dL) = {{c1::(1.34 x hemoglobin x saturation)}} + (0.003 x PO2)
cards.back: Hemoglobin in g per dL; 1.34 mL O2 per g is a common working value.
cards.quote: oxygen content = (1.34 x hemoglobin x saturation) + (0.003 x PO2)
cards.section: How much oxygen does the body use?

cards.front: An illustrative adult human has hemoglobin 14 g per dL, arterial saturation 96% and arterial PO2 90 mmHg. Using 1.34 mL O2 per g and 0.003 mL per dL per mmHg dissolved, what is the arterial oxygen content?
cards.back: Bound = 1.34 × 14 × 0.96 = 18.01 mL per dL; dissolved = 0.003 × 90 = 0.27 mL per dL; total about 18.3 mL O2 per dL.
cards.quote: bound = 1.34 x 15 x 0.98 = 19.70 mL per dL; dissolved = 0.003 x 100 = 0.30 mL per dL
cards.section: How much oxygen does the body use?

cards.front: An adult human has a cardiac output of 8.0 L per min, arterial oxygen content 19 mL per dL and mixed venous content 12 mL per dL. Calculate oxygen delivery and oxygen use.
cards.back: 8.0 L per min = 80 dL per min. Delivery = 80 × 19 = 1,520 mL O2 per min. Use (Fick) = 80 × (19 − 12) = 560 mL O2 per min.
cards.why: Convert litres to decilitres before multiplying by a per-dL content.
cards.quote: Delivery is 50 x 20.00 = 1,000 mL per min; use is 50 x 4.80 = 240 mL per min.
cards.section: How much oxygen does the body use?

cards.front: Arterial oxygen content is 19.0 mL per dL and mixed venous content is 11.4 mL per dL. What fraction of the oxygen offered did the tissues take, and how does it compare with the resting value of about a quarter?
cards.back: (19.0 − 11.4) / 19.0 = 7.6 / 19.0 = 40%, well above the resting 24%, so the tissues are drawing on the reserve.
cards.quote: The tissues took 4.80 / 20.00 = 24% of the oxygen offered.
cards.section: How much oxygen does the body use?

cards.front: Bohr found that carbon dioxide lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity. Why did his experiment leave open how it does so?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide also makes blood more acidic, so its own effect and the effect of acid were not separated.
cards.why: Later work showed both act: hydrogen ions and carbon dioxide bound to the protein.
cards.quote: Bohr's experiment showed that carbon dioxide lowers affinity, but not how, since carbon dioxide also makes blood more acidic.
cards.section: Shifting the curve: what the experiment left open

cards.front: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) is made in red cells from a side branch of {{c1::glycolysis}}.
cards.quote: BPG, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, is made in red cells from a side branch of glycolysis and acts inside them.
cards.section: Shifting the curve: what the experiment left open

cards.front: How does BPG raise hemoglobin's P50?
cards.back: It binds preferentially to the deoxygenated, low-affinity form, about one per four-chain hemoglobin, in the cavity between the beta chains. Favouring that form lowers affinity.
cards.quote: It binds preferentially to the deoxygenated, low-affinity form of hemoglobin, about one molecule per four-chain hemoglobin, in the cavity between the beta chains.
cards.section: Shifting the curve: what the experiment left open

cards.front: Name four changes that shift the oxygen dissociation curve left, toward higher affinity.
cards.back: Higher pH, less carbon dioxide, lower temperature, less BPG. The opposite changes shift it right (higher P50).
cards.quote: Higher pH, less carbon dioxide, lower temperature or less BPG shift the curve left, toward higher affinity.
cards.section: Shifting the curve: what the experiment left open

cards.front: Blood enters hard-working muscle, where carbon dioxide is high, pH is lower and temperature is higher. What happens to P50 and to oxygen release, and why?
cards.back: P50 rises (right shift), so at the same tissue PO2 saturation is lower and more oxygen is released. Loading in the lungs is barely affected, because the curve is flat there.
cards.why: Release = capacity × fall in saturation; a right shift widens that fall.
cards.quote: For oxygen it is the one idea at work: working tissue's carbon dioxide and acid widen the fall in saturation between lung and tissue.
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: In a hypothetical experiment, blood is equilibrated at PCO2 40 or 60 mmHg. At PO2 100 mmHg saturation is 97% versus 96%; at PO2 30 mmHg it is 57% versus 48%. What do the data show, and why does it matter for oxygen delivery?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide lowers affinity (a right shift), with a large effect in the unloading range and little on the loading plateau. So working tissue gets more oxygen while loading in the lungs is nearly unchanged.
cards.quote: a modest right shift costs little in the lungs

cards.front: What kind of oxygen supply suits a left-shifted (high-affinity) carrier? Give two examples.
cards.back: A supply that is not air in the lungs: another blood, as for fetal blood at the placenta, or blood feeding a store, as for myoglobin in muscle.
cards.quote: A left-shifted carrier suits a supply that is not air in the lungs
cards.section: Shifting the curve: what the experiment left open

cards.front: Fetal blood's dissociation curve lies left of the mother's, and fetal blood at the placenta has the lower PO2. How does the left shift help the fetus?
cards.back: At its lower PO2, fetal blood still reaches a high saturation, so it takes up more oxygen than adult blood would there. Net oxygen flow still runs down the PO2 difference, mother to fetus.
cards.quote: At its lower PO2, fetal blood still reaches a high saturation, so it takes up more oxygen than adult blood would there.
cards.section: Other carriers, other settings

cards.front: Why does human fetal blood bind oxygen more tightly than adult blood?
cards.back: Fetal hemoglobin has gamma chains in place of beta chains. It still binds BPG but responds less to it, a large part of its higher affinity.
cards.quote: Fetal hemoglobin, which has gamma chains in place of the adult beta chains, still binds BPG but responds less to it
cards.section: Other carriers, other settings

cards.front: BPG is stripped from purified adult and fetal hemoglobin and then added back at the same concentration. Adult hemoglobin's P50 rises about twofold; fetal hemoglobin's rises less. What does this show?
cards.back: Fetal hemoglobin responds less to BPG, which accounts for a large part of why fetal blood binds oxygen more tightly.
cards.quote: with BPG removed and then added back at the same concentration, adult hemoglobin's P50 rose about twofold while fetal hemoglobin's rose less.
cards.section: Other carriers, other settings

cards.front: How does myoglobin's oxygen binding differ from blood's, and when does it give up its oxygen?
cards.back: A single-chain store with a hyperbolic curve and a P50 roughly a tenth of blood's (horse myoglobin in solution versus modelled human blood). It takes oxygen from blood and releases it only when PO2 inside muscle fibres is very low, as in hard work.
cards.quote: It takes up oxygen from blood and gives it up only when the PO2 inside muscle fibres is very low, as in hard work.
cards.section: Other carriers, other settings

cards.front: Among mammals, how does blood P50 tend to vary with body size, and why might that fit?
cards.back: Small species tend to have higher P50 (lower affinity) than large ones, a loose trend that differs among lineages. Small animals use more oxygen per gram, and lower affinity favours unloading.
cards.quote: Among mammals, small species tend to have higher P50 values than large ones
cards.section: Other carriers, other settings

cards.front: What oxygen carrier do horseshoe crabs and octopuses use, and how does it differ from hemoglobin in red cells?
cards.back: Hemocyanin, a copper-containing protein dissolved in the blood rather than packed in cells. It is colourless without oxygen and blue with it.
cards.quote: Horseshoe crabs and octopuses carry oxygen on hemocyanin, a copper-containing protein dissolved in their blood instead of packed in cells.
cards.section: Other carriers, other settings

cards.front: Adult Antarctic icefish have no working hemoglobin. How do they carry oxygen, and what about their setting makes that workable?
cards.back: Oxygen travels dissolved in plasma. Near-freezing water holds more dissolved gas than warm water.
cards.quote: their oxygen travels dissolved in plasma, in near-freezing water that holds more dissolved gas than warm water.
cards.section: Other carriers, other settings

cards.front: Name the three forms in which carbon dioxide travels from resting tissue to the lungs, with their approximate shares.
cards.back: Bicarbonate about 85%, dissolved about 10%, on hemoglobin (carbamino) about 5%, per one careful review; shares depend on what is counted and change in exercise.
cards.why: Many textbooks give hemoglobin near a quarter, an older figure now thought too high.
cards.quote: For resting tissue, one careful review estimates about 85% as bicarbonate, 10% dissolved and 5% on hemoglobin
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: In red cells, carbonic anhydrase speeds the reaction CO2 + H2O ⇌ {{c1::H2CO3}} ⇌ H+ + HCO3-.
cards.quote: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3-
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: How is bicarbonate made from tissue carbon dioxide, and how does it get into plasma?
cards.back: Carbonic anhydrase in red cells speeds CO2 + H2O to H+ + HCO3-. The bicarbonate leaves the red cell in exchange for a chloride ion through a membrane exchanger.
cards.quote: The bicarbonate leaves the red cell in exchange for a chloride ion through a membrane exchanger (see membrane transport) and travels in plasma.
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: What happens to the hydrogen ions made with bicarbonate in tissue red cells, and how does that affect oxygen binding?
cards.back: Hemoglobin takes up most of them, acting as a buffer. That lowers its oxygen affinity in tissue capillaries, part of the Bohr effect.
cards.quote: Hemoglobin takes up most of the hydrogen ions, acting as a buffer; this is one way carbon dioxide lowers hemoglobin's affinity in tissue capillaries
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: Where on hemoglobin does carbon dioxide bind to form carbamino compounds?
cards.back: To the end amino groups of hemoglobin's chains, not to the iron where oxygen sits.
cards.quote: Some carbon dioxide binds directly to the end amino groups of hemoglobin's chains, forming carbamino compounds, not to the iron where oxygen sits.
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: Deoxygenated hemoglobin takes up hydrogen ions and forms carbamino compounds more readily than oxygenated hemoglobin. As blood loads oxygen in the lungs, does it hold more or less carbon dioxide at the same PCO2, and why?
cards.back: Less. Oxygen binding makes hemoglobin release hydrogen ions and carbamino CO2; the hydrogen ions turn bicarbonate back into CO2, which is breathed out. This is the Haldane effect.
cards.quote: at the same carbon dioxide pressure, deoxygenated blood carries more carbon dioxide than oxygenated blood
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: As blood unloads oxygen in a tissue capillary, what happens to the amount of bicarbonate it can form from the tissue's carbon dioxide, and why?
cards.back: It rises. Deoxygenated hemoglobin removes the H+ made with each bicarbonate, so the reaction runs further toward bicarbonate and more carbon dioxide is carried away.
cards.quote: deoxygenated hemoglobin removes the H+ made with each bicarbonate and lets the reaction run further to the right.
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: Explain how the Bohr and Haldane effects are one coupling seen from two sides, and how together they help gas exchange in working muscle and the lungs.
cards.back: Bohr: carbon dioxide and acid lower oxygen binding, so working tissue unloads more oxygen. Haldane: losing oxygen lets hemoglobin take up H+ and carbamino CO2, so tissue blood carries more CO2; in the lungs oxygen loading drives CO2 off.
cards.why: Both rest on deoxygenated hemoglobin binding H+ and CO2 more readily than oxygenated hemoglobin.
cards.quote: So the Bohr and Haldane effects are one coupling seen from each side
cards.section: Carrying carbon dioxide back

cards.front: With capacity 20.1 mL O2 per dL, standard blood is 97.7% saturated at 100 mmHg and 74.9% at 40 mmHg; right-shifted blood (P50 32) is 96.2% and 64.6%. Compare oxygen released from hemoglobin between 100 and 40 mmHg.
cards.back: Standard: 20.1 × (0.977 − 0.749) ≈ 4.6 mL per dL. Shifted: 20.1 × (0.962 − 0.646) ≈ 6.4 mL per dL, about two-fifths more, at a loading cost of only about 1.5 points.
cards.quote: The right shift costs about 1.5 points of loading but raises resting release by about two-fifths
cards.section: The films' carriers, by the numbers

cards.front: In the model, a one-site carrier with the same P50 as blood (26.8 mmHg) is 78.9% saturated at 100 mmHg and 42.7% at 20 mmHg; one with P50 3 mmHg is 97.1% and 87.0%. Why can neither match hemoglobin's sigmoid curve?
cards.back: The loose one loads only about four-fifths in the lungs and has far less reserve (about 7 against 13 mL per dL down to 20 mmHg). The tight one loads fully but releases under 1 mL per dL at rest.
cards.why: A one-site carrier cannot both load fully and unload a lot over this range; cooperative binding can.
cards.quote: The loose one-site carrier releases almost as much at rest (3.8 against 4.6 mL per dL) but leaves the lungs about four-fifths full
cards.section: The films' carriers, by the numbers

cards.front: A person's lung PO2 is low enough that arterial blood sits below the flat plateau of the curve. Predict whether a right shift costs more or less loading than it would at a lung PO2 of 100 mmHg, and why.
cards.back: More. Below about 60 mmHg the curve is no longer flat, so lowering affinity cuts arterial saturation noticeably and loading suffers.
cards.why: A modest right shift costs little only because lung blood normally sits on the flat plateau.
cards.quote: a large shift or a low lung PO2 would cost more.
cards.section: The films' carriers, by the numbers

cards.front: Design an experiment to tell whether fetal hemoglobin's higher oxygen affinity is built into the protein or comes from its response to BPG.
cards.back: Strip purified adult and fetal hemoglobin of BPG and organic phosphates; compare P50 (built-in affinity). Add back equal BPG at several concentrations and compare the rise in P50. Hold pH, temperature, buffer, salt and hemoglobin concentration equal; then check whole blood at 37 degrees C.
cards.quote: Strip purified adult and fetal hemoglobin of BPG and other organic phosphates
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A hypothetical adult hemoglobin variant binds BPG normally but responds to it much less, like fetal hemoglobin. Predict its P50 in red cells and its effect on unloading in resting tissue.
cards.back: Lower P50 (left shift, higher affinity), so less oxygen is released between lungs and tissue at the same PO2 values.
cards.why: BPG raises P50 by favouring the low-affinity form; a weaker response leaves affinity higher, as in fetal blood.
cards.quote: By favouring that form, it raises P50.
cards.section: Shifting the curve: what the experiment left open
